newsitem.title: UK: Dollar boosted by Rubin forex comment in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar boosted by Rubin forex comment in Europe.

text.p: The dollar strengthened its tone against the mark and yen in Europe's afternoon as U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said a strong dollar was in the U.S. interest and that Washington's dollar policy had not changed.

The dollar had spent most of the European session on a soft note and eased slightly after gaining on Rubin's comment as profit-taking kicked in, but traders said bullish dollar sentiment had been intact all the while.
"Short-term, people are going to take profits. But with higher U.S. interest rates, there's really only one direction the dollar can go," said one trader at a U.S. bank.

Rubin made his comments concerning the dollar in an interview with CNBC television, in which he also said exchange rates follow fundamentals and the U.S. has had strong economic fundamentals for the past four years, adding that this was being reflected by the dollar.
Meanwhile, he said Washington shared Japanese authorities' concern over the yen's recent drop against the dollar because of the impact on Japan's trade surplus.
Although dollar/yen dipped fleetingly on Rubin's reference to the yen, this sentiment was soon wiped out by the treasury secretary's other dollar-supportive comments.

The dollar was at 125.98/08 yen at 1555 GMT after rising to around 126.30 soon after Rubin's comments. It was still well short of the 56-month high of 127.19 it hit in overnight trade, and its late Wednesday European level of 126.93/98.

Dollar/mark also jumped on Rubin's statement, briefly spiking above 1.72 marks although it had subsided to 1.7173/80 by late trade. It hit a 37-month peak of 1.7272 overnight and had been at 1.7262/69 in late Wednesday trade.
The market was now focusing on U.S. March retail sales and producer prices due Friday for direction, said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives trading at the Cooperative Bank.
Despite some nervousness over the speed of the dollar's rally this week, fundamentals still pointed to a further rise in the dollar, albeit a slower one, analysts said.
"Looking at the state of play in Germany and the U.S., you see a different story in terms of economies," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi International.
"You might say what is necessary in Germany is a weaker currency, to try and offset what was an overvalued currency and weakness in the economy," he said.
Rubin's remarks helped revive the dollar sentiment that had been subdued earlier by comments from his Japanese counterpart.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the yen's recent fall against the dollar was excessive, and that Japan would deal decisively with excessive currency moves.
This was a hardening up of Mitsuzuka's stance from yesterday, when he had declined to say whether he thought the speed of the yen's drop at the time was excessive.

Mitsuzuka's comments were echoed by Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Finance Ministry's international finance bureau. Sakakibara said Japanese authorities may intervene if currency rates deviated greatly from fundamentals, adding that recent dollar/yen moves were not in line with fundamentals.

Elsewhere in the currency market, the mark softened against other European currencies as dollar/mark gained. The market was keeping watch over the political situation in Italy where the Senate was holding a vote of confidence on Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government, which he was expected to win.
The British pound also firmed against the mark, though it was still shy of the 4-1/2 year high of 2.7985 it hit overnight. Sterling/mark was at 2.7891/01 compared with late Wednesday's 2.7950/55.
